title: Scientists solve 1840s space weather mystery
gist: A Space Weather paper led by Lancaster University's Jim Wild shows that an 1871 Nature report of an 1841 geomagnetic storm delaying a train in Exeter was almost certainly a typo for October 1848, since the relevant rail line did not open until 1846. That makes a March 1847 Midland Railway telegraph disruption the earliest documented space-weather impact on technology; the article stresses a Carrington-scale storm today could seriously damage power grids and satellites.

insights.claim: The 1859 Carrington Event remains the most powerful geomagnetic storm on record, causing sparking and fires in telegraph stations, with some operators transmitting messages on auroral current alone after disconnecting power.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Benchmark event for stress-testing modern infrastructure resilience.

insights.claim: The 1871 Nature report of an October 1841 train delay in Exeter cannot be accurate, because the South Devon Railway section involved did not open until May 30, 1846.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Shows how uncritical reliance on single sources distorts risk-event baselines.

insights.claim: Greenwich magnetograms show no unusual activity on October 18, 1841, but strong geomagnetic activity around October 18, 1848, and railway timetables list a 10:05 pm Exeter express only in 1848-1849, so the date was likely a typo.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Cross-verifying data sources is key to accurate event histories.

insights.claim: With the 1841 account ruled out, the earliest documented space-weather impact on technology is a March 1847 incident of spontaneous currents disrupting Midland Railway telegraph systems during a brilliant aurora.

insights.so_what: Resets the historical baseline for technology-affecting geomagnetic storms.
